All representations start from the same time-frequency picture and differ in what they keep. Perceptual features and MFCCs condense each frame and segment into a few numbers that model how the ear hears; musical features add the structure that listeners recognize in music. Classifiers turn features into labels, first with hand-crafted features and small trees for two classes, then with networks that learn their features for hundreds of classes, and finally with CLAP, which labels and searches with free text. Transcription is the special case for speech: it turns audio into the richest description of all, text, but its errors fall on the names that users search for. Fingerprinting keeps the least, a sparse set of peak pairs, and is the only representation that names one exact recording under heavy distortion. The learned models did not make the hand-crafted ones obsolete: cost, explainability, small devices, and exact identification still favor them.

Perceptual features measure loudness, brightness, noisiness, and change per frame; segment statistics capture how these values vary. LSTER and HZCRR separate speech from music where the mean ZCR does not.

MFCCs model the ear in three steps: the mel filter bank follows its frequency resolution, the logarithm its loudness perception, and the cosine transform keeps the smooth spectral envelope in 13 coefficients, extended by their changes to 39 values.
Chroma describes pitch classes and the key independent of the octave; tempo comes from the periodicity of the onset strength, with octave errors as the typical failure.

Hand-crafted features with a small tree solve a two-class problem cheaply and transparently. Pretrained networks recognize hundreds of classes, and CLAP assigns labels and answers text queries without a classifier trained for them, but only among the prompts it is given. Classifiers must be evaluated on held-out recordings.

Transcription makes speech searchable as text. Weakly supervised encoder-decoder models such as Whisper and LLM-based recognizers transcribe many languages, but quality follows the amount of training data per language, dialects become translations, and names and rare terms fail most often. Hotwords at indexing time and phonetic matching at query time address these errors.

A fingerprint pairs spectrogram peaks into hashes, looks them up in an inverted file, and accepts a recording only if many matches agree on one time offset. It identifies recordings under heavy noise, but not songs in other performances.
